MAE PANER, TUTOL SA “BAWAL MARCOS RESIGN” RALLY NI KIKO DEE

Naglabas ng matapang na reaksiyon ang aktres at social activist na si Mae Paner kaugnay ng pahayag ni Francis Aquino Dee, co-convenor ng Tindig Pilipinas, na ipagbabawal ang panawagang “Marcos Resign” sa gaganaping Trillion Peso March sa EDSA.

Matatandaang sinabi ni Dee na hindi papayagan ang anumang panawagan na naglalayong pabagsakin ang isang halal na opisyal, dahil umano’y labag ito sa Konstitusyon.

Ngunit para kay Paner, tila taliwas ito sa diwa ng People Power, na siyang nagpatalsik sa diktadurya noong 1986.

“Ang unang EDSA People Power ang nagpatalsik sa mga tiwaling Marcos at naiupo ang Aquino.”

Dagdag pa niya:

“Bakit ni ayaw singilin ni Kiko Aquino Dee ang tiwaling Marcos sa EDSA@40?”

“Di ba sila nagnakaw? Nasoli ba?”

Kasunod nito, kinuwestiyon din niya ang pamumuno ni Pangulong  Marcos Jr.:

“Si BBM ba matino?”

At iniuugnay pa niya ito sa posibleng takot sa pulitikal na implikasyon:

“Fear of Sara?”

Sa huli, iginiit ni Paner na ang pagbabawal sa panawagang pagpapatalsik ay tila pagsampal sa diwa ng People Power:

“Di ba sampal ’yan sa pipol?”

Para kay Mae Paner, ang ganitong patakaran ay tila paglimot sa kasaysayan ng EDSA, na mismong mamamayan ang nagpatalsik sa isang rehimen na inakusahan ng katiwalian at pang-aabuso sa kapangyarihan.

Sa kanyang pananaw, ang tunay na diwa ng People Power ay paniningil sa mga may sala—kahit pa sila ay nakaupo sa pinakamataas na posisyon sa bansa.

#marcos #duterte #VPSaraDuterte #DavaoCity #AngBalitaNgayonFB

In 1934, a young schoolteacher from rural West Virginia traded her chalkboard for an Army nurse's uniform. Ruby Bradley would retire 29 years later as a Colonel—and one of the most decorated women in U.S. history.
Ruby was born in 1907 on a farm near Spencer, West Virginia, in a world that expected little from Appalachian girls. She taught in one-room schoolhouses, but she wanted a bigger fight. She became a surgical nurse, and at 26, she joined the U.S. Army.
For seven quiet years, she worked in hospitals.
Then came World War II.
Stationed in the Philippines, Bradley tried to escape the Japanese invasion-but was captured in December 1941, becoming one of the first American Army nurse POWs of the war. She would spend 37 months as a prisoner.
Food was half a cup of rice a day. Supplies were nonexistent. Yet Ruby helped build a secret clinic, smuggled instruments, and performed surgery with improvised tools. She assisted in over 200 operations and delivered 13 babies.
And she gave away her food-saving starving children instead of herself. Her uniform hung loose as she dropped to 84 pounds, perfect for hiding stolen medicine and food. POWs called her and the other nurses "Angels in Fatigues." After liberation in 1945, most would have gone home.

Ruby reenlisted.
During the Korean War, now a Major, she supervised frontline evacuation hospitals under fire. When Chinese forces surrounded her position, she refused to board the rescue plane until every wounded soldier was loaded first. She jumped aboard last—just as her ambulance exploded behind her.
Bradley rose to Chief Nurse of the Eighth Army, overseeing 500 nurses. In 1958, she became a Colonel-only the third woman in Army history to reach that rank. She retired in 1963 with 34 decorations, including two Legions of Merit, two Bronze Stars, and the Florence Nightingale Medal.
Ruby went back to West Virginia-not as a legend, but as a working nurse.
She died in 2002 at age 94 and received full honors at Arlington National Cemetery: horse-drawn caisson, military band, rifle salute.
Asked once about heroism, Ruby refused the title:
"It was just all in a day's work. I was just an Army nurse."
But history knows better.
She fed the starving.
She saved the wounded.
She never ran.
Sometimes, courage wears fatigues— and just keeps going 🙏
